pr_body:
Adds middleware for decompressing HTTP requests.

### Problem
In the past, the developer of the server would need to manually handle requests with compressed content by checking if a request was compressed and then decompressing the request body stream as appropriate.  

### Solution
This middleware uses the `Content-Encoding` header automatically identify and decompress requests with compressed content, so that the developer of the server does not need to handle this themselves.

The request decompression middleware is added using the `UseRequestDecompression` extension method for `IApplicationBuilder` and the `AddRequestDecompression` extension method for `IServiceCollection`.

### Supported Content Encodings
Support for Brotli (`br`), Deflate (`deflate`), and GZip (`gzip`) are included out of the box.

Support for other content encodings can be added by registering a custom decompression provider class, which implements the `IDecompressionProvider` interface, along with a `Content-Encoding` header value in `RequestDecompressionOptions`.

### Request Size Limits
The request body size limit enforced by the server (`MaxRequestBodySize`) and/or the endpoint (`RequestSizeLimitAttribute`) will also be enforced on the decompressed request body.

If the amount of data read from the decompressed request body exceeds the size limit, an `InvalidOperationException` is thrown to prevent any more data from being read. This protects against the threat of uncontrolled resource consumption from [zip bombs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zip_bomb)

### Edge Cases
- If a request uses an unsupported `Content-Encoding` or has multiple encodings, an appropriate message will be logged, and the request will be passed on without being decompressed.
- If the compressed content is invalid, an exception will be thrown when attempting to read the (decompressed) request body stream.

Fixes #40080

Random thought: what if we designed the feature like so: https://gist.github.com/pranavkm/8932a862a701061f43b6e64cc0b18931. It removes some of the newly introduced types at the expense of slightly more code in each of the compression providers.

@sebastienros / @Tratcher?

> @sebastienros / @Tratcher?

It's simpler, but you loose things like DI and logging support for providers. Is the current structure really too complex?

@pranavkm Looks great! I'll update the middleware to use this design.

One question: In the `RequestDecompressionMiddleware` example above, how specifically should the size limit be pulled from the `RequestSizeLimitAttribute` (since its `_bytes` property is private)? I noticed that this value is public on the `RequestSizeLimitFilter` that it creates, but this class isn't accessible. Is there another way to get this value from the endpoint?

If we take the `IRequestSizeLimitMetadata` approach, should we just update the `EndpointRoutingMiddleware` to do what the `RequestSizeLimitFilter` currently does and set `IHttpMaxRequestBodySizeFeature.MaxRequestBodySize` based on the metadata? The upside is that the attribute would now work as metadata for all endpoints including minimal route handlers.

> should we just update the EndpointRoutingMiddleware to do what the RequestSizeLimitFilter currently does and set IHttpMaxRequestBodySizeFeature.MaxRequestBodySize based on the metadata?

That's an interesting idea. We'd spoken about using the metadata at callsites (e.g. `ReadFormAsync` \ multipart reader APIs using the metadata from the passed in HttpContext), but using the routing middleware hadn't come up. It's certainly a convenient place to do it, but fails the purity of concerns test (what does routing care about request body limits). 

Perhaps we can tackle that separately from this PR?

> Perhaps we can tackle that separately from this PR?

Maybe. It does feel wrong to enforce the limit set by `RequestSizeLimitAttribute`s on minimal route handlers if request decompression is used but not otherwise.

issue_context.title: RequestDecompression middleware
issue_context.body:
The same way we have a `ResponseCompression` middleware we should have a `RequestDecompression` one that automatically decompress the requests containing `Content-Encoding` with supported formats (gzip, deflate, brotli, ...). Based on the same extensible compression factories.

Scenario: a client sends files to a server using gzip compressed streams. The developer of the server application doesn't have to care about how to decrompress the body.

I've added the following as a remark to the doc comments for `DisableRequestSizeLimitAttribute`:

`Disabling the request body size limit can be a security concern in regards to uncontrolled resource consumption, particularly if the request body is being buffered.`

Let me know if there's anything that you'd like me to add or change.

review_comments: @Tratcher do the servers throw at the size limit? Essentially should this be a `>=` check?
This is fine, throwing only if the limit is exceeded makes sense.
I think you'll have to await this to ensure the stream does not get disposed before this is completed. It might be easier to use a using block within this method call
Better to move the using/disposal of the decompression stream into InvokeCore's finally block.
I haven't think this through completely yet but with this implementation `EnableBuffering` must be always used after this middleware to work correctly, right?
EnableBuffering could be used before or after, it depends on what you're trying to do. It's true that the decompression stream wouldn't be seekable after this middleware without additional buffering.

> It's true that the decompression stream wouldn't be seekable after this middleware without additional buffering.

I'm still not sure of my suggestion but should at least `CanSeek`, `Length` and `Position` return the `_innerStream` results instead of `false` and throwing exceptions?
Sure, this wrapper should delegate, though the decompression streams will return the same result.
I've updated `CanSeek`, `Length`, and `Position` to return the `_innerStream`'s result. I also did the same with `Seek` and `SetLength` for sake of consistency.

We should set `IHttpMaxRequestBodySizeFeature.MaxRequestBodySize` to the limit read from `IRequestSizeLimitMetadata.MaxRequestBodySize` like in [MVC's RequestSizeLimitFilter](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/3ea008c80d5cc63de7f90ddfd6823b7b006251ff/src/Mvc/Mvc.Core/src/Filters/RequestSizeLimitFilter.cs#L60-L61). Otherwise, requests under the specified size limit might still be rejected because of the server's limits on the compressed stream. This is [30 MB by default in Kestrel](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.aspnetcore.server.kestrel.core.kestrelserverlimits.maxrequestbodysize?view=aspnetcore-6.0#definition).

It will be redundant in the MVC case, but we'll remove this part of the logic from this middleware once we address #40452. We might remove the `RequestSizeLimitFilter` as well.

Also, we should do the `IHttpMaxRequestBodySizeFeature.MaxRequestBodySize` setting logic whether or not `decompressionStream is null`. It's a little weird, but once we start enforcing the request size limit to compressed requests to a given endpoint, we really should enforce the request size limit on all requests to that endpoint. It's not called the `CompressedRequestSizeLimitAttribute` after all.
If `IRequestSizeLimitMetadata` is null, I'm assuming we should leave `IHttpMaxRequestBodySizeFeature.MaxRequestBodySize` unchanged, correct?
I've updated this to set `IHttpMaxRequestBodySizeFeature.MaxRequestBodySize` using `IRequestSizeLimitMetdata.MaxRequestBodySize`.

> If `IRequestSizeLimitMetadata` is null, I'm assuming we should leave `IHttpMaxRequestBodySizeFeature.MaxRequestBodySize` unchanged, correct?

No. If `IRequestSizeLimitMetadata` is not present, we should leave `IHttpMaxRequestBodySizeFeature.MaxRequestBodySize` unchanged like you say because that means the endpoint has no attribute changing things one way or the other.

If `IRequestSizeLimitMetadata` is present and `IRequestSizeLimitMetadata.MaxRequestBodySize` is null, that means that `[DisableRequestSizeLimit]` or other metadata trying to do the same thing has been applied to the endpoint. In that case, we should ignore the initial default value of `IHttpMaxRequestBodySizeFeature.MaxRequestBodySize`. Instead of getting the value from the feature, we should set the value on the feature to null so the server doesn't limit the size of the request body before it gets to the decompression middleware.

In fact, we should *always* set `IHttpMaxRequestBodySizeFeature.MaxRequestBodySize` to `IRequestSizeLimitMetadata.MaxRequestBodySize` if `IRequestSizeLimitMetadata` exists. You could have a similar problem with the server limiting the size of the body before it gets to the decompression middleware even if the limit was set to a finite value like 1 GB.

Gotcha! This is how I setup the logic in the current implementation. 

I was specifically referring to the situation where the `IRequestSizeLimitMetadata` itself was null (i.e. the metadata was not present). I should have clarified this better in my original question.

So for `IRequestSizeLimitMetadata` to work properly this middleware should be placed after `UseRouting`. Why not pass `HttpContext` to the stream and get `sizeLimit` on first read? This way at least if first read is happened after `UseRouting` we have the `IRequestSizeLimitMetadata`.
We're looking at https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/40452 as a way to enforce the attribute uniformly across the stack. For now, this implementation should suffice

@Tratcher @pranavkm any thoughts on [this comment](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/40279#discussion_r810507794), on not creating `SizeLimitedStream` for known encodings to prevent allocation on each request?
What do known encodings have to do with it? We should always be enforcing a limit on the decompressed request body.

[Here ](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/40279#discussion_r810507794) I was saying that for known encodings, instead of creating an instance of `SizedLimitStream` and pass an instance of `GZipStream` in its ctor, we write a new class called `SizedLimitGZipStream` which inherits `GZipStream` and check the size on its Read method. This way instead of allocating two instances of `GZipSteam` and `SizedLimitStream` we only allocate one `SizedLimitGZipStream`. 

The _known encoding_ part is for that we don't know if the stream returning from the provider is checking the size, so (here comes the ugly part!) `SizedLimitGZipStream` should also implement a marker interface, so the middleware only wrap the stream in `SizedLimitStream` if the stream is not implementing the marker interface. The marker interface could be internal of course.
That's going to be a lot of extra code to save that allocation. Let's not for now.
I blame @davidfowl for making me think this way. I've got _allocaphobia_ (fear of allocation). 😅
![JackNicholsonYesGIF](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/95136/156197037-488dafea-a627-4442-8ff2-d5adadcacc6d.gif)
We can optimize after the feature works if the gains show its worth it. I'm all about not allocating per request.

Does this interface really need the 3 separate methods? Right now the Content-Encoding header is checked multiple times and look-up for `IDecompressionProvider` id done twice in `IsContentEncodingSupported` and `GetDecompressionProvider`.

I think the `IDecompressionProvider? GetDecompressionProvider(HttpContext context)` method should be enough.
I've moved consolidated all the checks into `GetDecompressionProvider` and removed the other methods on the interface.
